Both meanings of "alight" share one beautiful underlying idea: something in motion comes gently to rest in a specific place. Keep that image in your mind — it ties everything together.
Meaning 1 — To land and settle on a surface

This is the most physical meaning. It describes the moment when something — most commonly a bird or insect — comes down through the air and settles on a spot.

  • A sparrow alighted on the fence post.
  • The butterfly alighted on the rose.
  • Snowflakes alighted on her coat.

It is also used for a person stepping off a vehicle — a bus, train, or carriage. This use is formal and common in British English, especially in transport announcements.

  • Passengers should alight at the next stop.
  • She alighted from the train and looked around the unfamiliar station.

In both cases — bird landing, person stepping off — the action is the same in spirit: movement ends, and something comes to rest somewhere.
Meaning 2 — To come across something, often by chance

This meaning is mental rather than physical. When your eyes or mind "alight on" something, you suddenly notice it or discover it — often unexpectedly, as if you stumbled upon it without planning to.

Think of your attention as a bird flying around a room — and then suddenly landing on one particular thing. That landing is what "alight on" means here.

  • Her eyes alighted on a dusty envelope at the back of the drawer.
  • While flipping through the book, he alighted on a passage that changed his thinking.
  • After hours of searching, she finally alighted on the perfect solution.

Notice that this meaning almost always uses the preposition "on" or "upon" — you alight on something, or alight upon something.

• Alight on / alight upon → used for both meanings (landing on a surface, or noticing something)
  • Alight from → used specifically for stepping off a vehicle
Register — when is this word used?

"Alight" as a verb is literary and formal. You will rarely hear it in everyday conversation. It lives mostly in literature, formal writing, and official announcements. In casual speech, people simply say:

  • landed on — instead of alighted on (for birds/insects)
  • got off — instead of alighted from (for vehicles)
  • noticed or came across — instead of alighted on (for discovering something)

So when you encounter "alight" as a verb, it is almost always a deliberate, stylish word choice — the writer wants a sense of gentleness, precision, or elegance.
Do not confuse it with the adjective "alight"

The word "alight" is also commonly used as an adjective, and it means something completely different — on fire, or glowing with light. This can trip up learners.

  • The building was alight. (= on fire)
  • Her face was alight with happiness. (= glowing, radiant)

The context will always make it clear. If something or someone is doing the action, it is the verb. If the word is describing a state, it is the adjective. You will never genuinely confuse the two once you understand both.
A note on the past tense

The standard past tense is alighted.

  • The bird alighted on the branch. ✓

In older or very literary texts, you may occasionally see alit used as an irregular past tense form. It is rare and old-fashioned, but worth knowing so it does not surprise you.

  • The bird alit on the branch. (old-fashioned)
